Time in view for an aircraft

Source: R/availability.R
view_window_aerial.Rd

Computes the window for availability() for an observer looking through the side window of an aircraft. The field of view is a wedge running forward and aft of perpendicular, so time in view grows with perpendicular distance. This is the usual geometry for an aerial line-transect survey.

Usage

view_window_aerial(trackline, speed, angle = NULL, slope = NULL, distance = 0)

Arguments

trackline

Numeric. Time in view at the trackline, \(\alpha\), in seconds. Must not be negative.

speed

Numeric. Ground speed, in metres per second. Must be positive.

angle

Numeric or NULL (default). Viewing half-angle \(\theta\), in degrees from perpendicular: the view runs angle forward and angle aft. Must be above 0 and below 90. Give this or slope, not both.

slope

Numeric or NULL (default). Seconds in view gained per metre of perpendicular distance, \(2 \tan\theta / v\), if calibrated directly. Must not be negative. Give this or angle, not both.

distance

Numeric. Perpendicular distance, in metres. Default 0. Must not be negative.

Value

A numeric vector of windows in seconds.

How it works

Following the linear form fitted by Ganley et al. (2019), for a time in view \(\alpha\) at the trackline, a viewing half-angle \(\theta\) forward of perpendicular and the same aft, and ground speed \(v\):

$$t(x) = \alpha + \frac{2 x \tan\theta}{v}$$

A point at perpendicular distance \(x\) enters the wedge \(x \tan\theta\) ahead of abeam and leaves \(x \tan\theta\) behind, so it is in view for an extra \(2 x \tan\theta\) of track.

  1. Exactly one of angle and slope must be given.

  2. If angle is given, the slope is computed as \(2 \tan\theta / v\) seconds per metre.

  3. The window is trackline + distance * slope.

Calibrating the inputs

Measured values are better than derived ones. Ganley et al. (2019) flew past a navigation buoy and timed it through the field of view. For a Cessna Skymaster at 185 km/h and 228 or 304 m altitude, they found 51.22 s in view at the effective trackline and a slope of about 0.03 s per metre. The two altitudes did not differ detectably.

Their effective trackline is at 100 m, not 0 m, because the aircraft's flat windows leave a blind spot beneath it; their data were left-truncated at 100 m for that reason. At the fitting end the same blind spot is handled by sweep_models(left = ) or the gamma key.

References

Ganley, L.C., Brault, S. and Mayo, C.A. (2019) What we see is not what there is: estimating North Atlantic right whale Eubalaena glacialis local abundance. Endangered Species Research 38:101-113. doi:10.3354/esr00938

See also

availability(), view_window(), view_window_vessel(), ganley_availability

Examples

# Ganley et al.'s Skymaster, calibrated directly: 51.22 s at the trackline,
# plus about 0.03 s per metre
view_window_aerial(trackline = 51.22, speed = 51.4, slope = 0.03,
                   distance = c(0, 1000, 3000))
#> [1]  51.22  81.22 141.22

# The same from a half-angle: 2 * tan(37.6 deg) / 51.4 is about 0.03 s/m
view_window_aerial(trackline = 51.22, speed = 51.4, angle = 37.6,
                   distance = c(0, 1000, 3000))
#> [1]  51.22000  81.18512 141.11537
